title: Defending against SIM-swap attacks
body_md:
## A phone number is a recovery route

In a SIM swap or number-port attack, someone persuades a carrier to move your number to a SIM or account they control. Your own phone may lose mobile service. Calls and SMS sent to that number can reach the attacker, including sign-in and password-reset codes. The attacker may still need a password, an existing session or a weak recovery flow: number control alone does not automatically open every account. A no-service icon also has innocent causes such as an outage, a damaged SIM or a billing issue. Treat it as a time-sensitive signal to verify.

An account PIN or transfer lock may make unauthorized changes harder, but carrier offerings and verification procedures differ. The PIN is not the same as the PIN that unlocks your phone's SIM. Use your carrier's official app or a number from a bill or known website to ask: which changes require the account PIN, is porting separately locked, and how will I be alerted? Keep the carrier account password and recovery email secure. Never disclose a one-time carrier code to an incoming caller claiming to be support.

## Separate your valuable accounts from SMS

Review the primary email first: it often resets other accounts. Where supported, use a passkey or security key, or an authenticator app instead of SMS. An authenticator app resists number theft, although a code can still be phished; a passkey or security key can resist phishing when correctly used. Save backup codes offline or in a protected manager, and test that you can recover without the phone number. Some banks require SMS or phone recovery; document that limitation and ask the bank what extra safeguards it offers. Removing your number from every service is not always possible or desirable.

## When service disappears

Check whether other nearby users of the same carrier are also affected and whether Wi-Fi still works. If the loss is unexplained, contact the carrier immediately from a different phone or trusted internet connection using a known channel. Ask if a SIM change or port was requested, request a block/reversal if unauthorized, and record the case reference. Independently open your email and financial services on a trusted device to review sign-ins and transactions. If you see unauthorized activity, use each provider's fraud channel quickly; change credentials and sessions as their guidance permits. Preserve alerts and times privately. Do not paste codes or account details into an educational exercise. After the number is restored, revisit recovery methods; a simple replacement SIM does not undo account changes already made.

widget_config.goal: Reduce dependence on a phone number for account recovery and respond to an unexplained loss of service without assuming it is an attack.
widget_config.today_action: In your carrier’s official app or help channel, check whether an account PIN, port lock or transfer alert exists. Then check the recovery and MFA options of your primary email account.
widget_config.scope: Carrier features and reporting routes vary by country and operator; examples are synthetic. FTC guidance is US-facing and dated 2019, so verify current local carrier procedures as of 2026-10-20.

sources.title: FTC SIM swap consumer alert
sources.scope: US consumer advice published 2019; mechanism, account PIN, immediate carrier contact.

sources.title: FTC two-factor authentication guide
sources.scope: US general account guidance; SMS can be diverted in SIM swap.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B authenticators
sources.scope: US federal technical standard: manually entered OTP is not phishing-resistant; WebAuthn is an example of verifier-name binding.

blocks.title: Unexpected silence after a carrier notice
blocks.situation: Synthetic: Nika’s phone shows no service and her email on Wi-Fi shows a carrier notice about a new SIM; a payment alert follows.
blocks.analysis: The combined signals justify urgent independent calls to the carrier and bank while she checks email access on a trusted device. She records times; she does not rely on the contact number inside a suspicious message. The alert alone does not prove the payment completed.

blocks.title: A planned eSIM transfer
blocks.situation: Synthetic: Pavel moved his eSIM to a replacement phone minutes ago. The old handset loses service; the new handset has signal and the carrier’s official app shows the initiated transfer.
blocks.analysis: The timing and independently checked status explain the symptom. Pavel still confirms his accounts work and that no other transfer is pending; he does not report a crime merely because the old SIM stopped working.

blocks.title: Recover from a number-change alert
blocks.setup: Synthetic exercise: a phone loses service during a workday. Contacting the carrier now or waiting changes the timing of the next decision; no real account is used.

steps.prompt: Your phone says “no service” while a colleague on the same carrier has signal. First move?

choices.text: Contact the carrier through a saved number or official app over Wi-Fi.
choices.consequence: You can learn whether a SIM change exists quickly.
choices.explanation: Verify through a trusted channel before assuming the cause.

choices.consequence: An unauthorized transfer could continue unchecked.
choices.explanation: A quick check is proportionate even if it proves to be an outage.

steps.prompt: The carrier confirms a transfer you did not request. What do you ask?

choices.text: Ask only for a replacement handset.
choices.consequence: The unauthorized transfer and account access remain unresolved.
choices.explanation: Hardware replacement does not correct carrier records.

choices.text: Block or reverse it, secure the carrier account and get a case reference.
choices.consequence: The number may be recovered and the timeline documented.
choices.explanation: Carrier action limits continuing number control; keep a record.

steps.prompt: The next morning, service is still absent. You contact the carrier through its official channel; it confirms a transfer you did not request. What do you ask now?

choices.text: Ask only for a replacement handset.
choices.consequence: After the lost day, the unauthorized transfer remains unresolved.
choices.explanation: Hardware replacement does not correct carrier records.

choices.text: Block or reverse it, secure the carrier account and get a case reference.
choices.consequence: The carrier can act, but the lost day cannot be recovered; you document the timeline.
choices.explanation: Carrier action limits continuing number control; keep a record.

steps.prompt: Independently, the bank app on a trusted laptop shows an unfamiliar transfer request. What next?

choices.text: Tell the caller who claims to be bank support the SMS code.
choices.consequence: A scammer may gain another way into the account.
choices.explanation: Inbound identity claims do not authorize code disclosure.

choices.text: Use the bank’s known fraud channel, protect email, and preserve alerts.
choices.consequence: Providers can act while evidence remains available.
choices.explanation: Account containment and financial response run alongside carrier recovery.

steps.prompt: Whether service returns soon or later, what follow-up reduces the risk to your accounts?

choices.text: Review email recovery/MFA, available carrier locks, sessions and affected accounts.
choices.consequence: You address paths the attacker may have touched.
choices.explanation: Restoring signal alone does not restore account integrity.

choices.text: Assume carrier recovery will make every account safe.
choices.consequence: Changed credentials or sessions may remain after the number returns.
choices.explanation: Account state must be checked separately from SIM state.

blocks.debrief: Replay both routes: waiting loses time, but every route still needs carrier recovery and separate account and financial checks.

questions.prompt: A phone loses mobile service after you initiated an eSIM move. What is the sound conclusion?

choices.text: Check the new device and official transfer status before escalating.
choices.explanation: An expected transfer can explain the symptom; verify it.

choices.text: Every loss of signal is a confirmed attack.
choices.explanation: Outages and planned changes also occur.

questions.prompt: What can an account PIN do?

choices.text: Make number transfer technically impossible everywhere.
choices.explanation: No universal lock or perfect procedure exists.

choices.text: Add a carrier-side obstacle if supported, without guaranteeing safety.
choices.explanation: The carrier may require it for changes; procedures vary.

questions.prompt: Why move primary email away from SMS MFA?

choices.text: A stolen number could receive codes or resets; another factor breaks that dependency.
choices.explanation: Email often controls recovery of other services.

choices.text: Because an authenticator code can never be phished.
choices.explanation: App-generated codes can still be entered into a fake site.

questions.prompt: After the carrier reverses a swap, what remains to check?

choices.explanation: Signal restoration does not undo account changes.

choices.text: Sessions, recovery settings and transactions on affected services.
choices.explanation: The attacker may have changed account state while holding the number.
